# Results — Study 427 (Rate of Change)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **ROC, the
oldest momentum oscillator, beats holding by going long when price is rising and stepping aside
when it falls** — tested as a daily **long/flat** timing rule on SPY. We race its **net,
excess-vs-excess** Sharpe against buy-and-hold, run the decisive HAC *t* on the **difference**
(ROC minus hold), a circular-permutation placebo on the timing, a cost sweep, and a head-to-head
against the obvious simpler rules (SMA(200), MACD, RSI). Offline & deterministic once cached;
run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily **total-return** closes for **SPY** (`auto_adjust=True`; splits + dividends folded in) |
| As-of | **2026-06-24** (pull); run **pinned to the last complete month**, 2026-05-29 |
| Window | 1993-01-29 → **2026-05-29** (8,390 bars; **33.3** calendar / 32.8 traded years) |
| Fingerprint | close-series sha1[:12] = **`f3fa058adfc8`** |
| Signal / lag | ROC over **126** trading days; long when ROC > 0, else flat (cash). Signal at close *t*, earns *t+1* — **one** `shift`, applied once |
| Costs / risk-free | **1 bp** one-way × \|Δposition\| × NAV (turnover = one-way × NAV); excess Sharpe uses a flat **2%/yr** risk-free, both legs |

> **No survivorship, no panel.** A single liquid ETF on its full history — the cleanest possible
> tape for a single-asset timing rule. Price series is **total-return** (dividends in), so the
> buy-and-hold benchmark is the honest one.

## The race — ROC long/flat vs buy-and-hold

| rule | excess Sharpe | net CAGR | worst drawdown | HAC *t* (own) | turnover/yr | exposure |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **ROC(126) long/flat** | **0.591** | **8.8%** | **−31%** | +3.71 | 6.6 | 0.76 |
| Buy & hold | 0.542 | 10.9% | −55% | +3.64 | 0.0 | 1.00 |

ROC's *standalone* excess Sharpe (0.591) nudges past buy-and-hold's (0.542) and its HAC *t*
(+3.71) clears the t≥2 bar — **but so does buy-and-hold's** (+3.64). That *t* is the equity
premium, not indicator skill: a rule that is long ~76% of a 33-year bull market will always look
significant. ROC's actual **return is lower** (8.8% vs 10.9%/yr); the only thing it buys is a
shallower drawdown (−31% vs −55%).

## The decisive test — does ROC *add* anything over holding?

The honest Signal number strips the beta out: the HAC *t* on the daily **difference**
ROC − buy-and-hold (net of costs).

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| ROC minus buy-and-hold | **−2.97%/yr** |
| HAC *t* on the difference | **−1.47** |
| break-even cost vs hold's CAGR | **0.0 bps** (ROC trails hold even at zero cost) |

The incremental edge is **negative and statistically insignificant**. ROC does **not** beat
buy-and-hold — it gives up ~3%/yr of return. There is no cost low enough to rescue it (its
zero-cost CAGR is already below hold's), so the break-even solve returns 0.

## Permutation placebo — does the *timing* carry information?

Circular-shift the realised position vector 5,000 times (same exposure, same turnover, random
alignment) and re-race the Sharpe:

| quantity | value |
|---|--:|
| observed excess Sharpe | 0.591 |
| permutation *p* | **0.034** |

The timing is **not** pure noise (*p* = 0.034) — stepping aside in deep down-trends genuinely
helps *risk-adjusted* return. But "beats a random schedule of the same exposure" is far weaker
than "beats buy-and-hold," which the difference-*t* already rejects. The information is real and
tiny, and it shows up as **lower drawdown**, not higher return.

## Window robustness — no lookback rescues it

| ROC lookback | excess Sharpe | net CAGR | Δ vs hold | HAC *t* (difference) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 21 | 0.264 | 4.4% | −7.10%/yr | −3.28 |
| 63 | 0.456 | 6.8% | −4.91%/yr | −2.29 |
| **126** | **0.591** | **8.8%** | **−2.97%/yr** | **−1.47** |
| 252 | 0.610 | 10.0% | −1.62%/yr | −0.87 |

The difference vs hold is **negative at every window** — worst at short lookbacks (whipsaw),
merely converging toward hold at long ones (by being invested more). There is no magic *N*.

## Cost sweep — costs are a red herring

| one-way cost | net excess Sharpe | net CAGR |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0 bps | 0.596 | 8.88% |
| 1 bp | 0.591 | 8.81% |
| 2 bp | 0.586 | 8.73% |
| 5 bp | 0.569 | 8.52% |
| 10 bp | 0.542 | 8.16% |

At ~7 round trips a year the net Sharpe barely moves from 1 to 10 bps. The rule's failure is
**structural** (no excess return), not **frictional** (costs). The long/short variant (short when
ROC < 0) is strictly worse: Sharpe 0.225, CAGR 4.6%, Δ vs hold −5.94%/yr (*t* = −1.47) — shorting
a market with a secular upward drift is a losing add-on.

## The rivals race — is the ROC *formula* special?

Same tape, same lag, same costs, same risk-free:

| rule | excess Sharpe | net CAGR | worst drawdown | HAC *t* | turnover/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Buy & hold | 0.542 | 10.9% | −55% | +3.64 | 0.0 |
| **ROC(126)** | **0.591** | 8.8% | −31% | +3.71 | 6.6 |
| **SMA(200)** | **0.580** | 8.6% | −28% | +3.55 | 6.6 |
| MACD(12,26,9) | 0.244 | 4.2% | −39% | +1.52 | 21.4 |
| RSI(14)>50 | 0.280 | 4.6% | −44% | +1.67 | 26.7 |

ROC(126) and a plain **200-day moving-average cross** are a **dead heat** (0.591 vs 0.580); both
beat the higher-churn MACD/RSI rules, which trade 3–4× as often and earn less. The benefit
credited to ROC is the **shared** "stay-long-in-uptrends" trend filter — the specific oscillator
is interchangeable.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness *can* detect a real timing edge

On a deterministic **regime-switching** tape (persistent up/down trends a momentum filter should
ride), the difference-vs-hold test behaves exactly as it must:

| planted edge | ROC Sharpe | hold Sharpe | Δ vs hold | HAC *t* (difference) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.0** (no trend) | −0.29 | −0.11 | −1.3%/yr | **−0.57** |
| **+0.5** (real trend) | +4.83 | −0.15 | +76.0%/yr | **+11.01** |

With **no** planted trend the difference-*t* sits at −0.57 (the harness does **not** manufacture
an edge from noise); with a real persistent trend it jumps to +11.01 (ROC genuinely beats hold).
The machinery can see a timing edge when one exists — so the real-tape **null** is a finding, not
a broken pipeline.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** ROC's own excess Sharpe **0.591** (HAC *t* = 3.71) clears t≥2 but is
  **beta** (hold's *t* = 3.64, same machinery). The incremental edge over hold is **−2.97%/yr at
  HAC *t* = −1.47** — negative, insignificant. The timing carries *some* information vs a random
  schedule (placebo *p* = 0.034) but manifests as risk-reduction, not alpha. **WEAK, not REAL** —
  it does not clear the t≥2 bar on the only number that matters (the difference vs hold).
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** ROC **lowers** CAGR (8.8% vs 10.9%); its sole deliverable is drawdown
  (−31% vs −55%), which a 200-day SMA delivers identically. No incremental return to harvest or
  scale — operationally trivial, economically empty.
- **"A better momentum tool"? — MISATTRIBUTED.** ROC(126) (0.591) ties SMA(200) (0.580); the
  benefit is the shared trend filter, not the ROC formula. The credit is mis-assigned to the
  indicator — any simple trend rule does the same job.
